Beth-nimrah
beth-NIM-ruh
proper noun
Hebrew Beth-Nimrah, “house of sweet water” or “house of the leopard,” a fenced city built by Gad in the valley.

📖 Biblical Definition

Beth-nimrah was a city in the valley east of the Jordan, in the well-watered land that the children of Gad asked for their inheritance and built up for themselves. When Reuben and Gad received their portion in the country of Sihon, the children of Gad built Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran as fenced cities, with folds for their sheep (Num 32:36). The town lay in the rich valley near the Jordan, named among the cities of the rest of the kingdom of Sihon that fell to Gad, from the valley up to the edge of the sea of Chinnereth (Josh 13:27). Its name is read as “house of sweet water,” fitting a place of springs and good pasture, or “house of the leopard,” perhaps for the wild beasts of the thickets along the river. Beth-nimrah is little mentioned, yet it stands among the fenced cities and sheepfolds that the eastern tribes built for their families and flocks before they crossed over armed to fight for their brethren’s inheritance. It witnesses the settled provision the LORD made for His people in the good land east of Jordan, and the order by which they housed their little ones and their cattle in safety before going to war — care for the household joined to readiness for the battle.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A fenced city built by Gad in the valley east of Jordan, in a land of springs and good pasture.

expand to see more

BETH-NIMRAH, a fenced city in the valley east of the Jordan.

The children of Gad built it with folds for their sheep (Num 32:36).

It lay in the rest of the kingdom of Sihon that fell to Gad (Josh 13:27).

Its name signifies “house of sweet water” or “house of the leopard.”

It was a place of springs and good pasture near the Jordan.

📖 Key Scripture

Num 32:36 — "And Bethnimrah, and Bethharan, fenced cities: and folds for sheep."

Josh 13:27 — "And in the valley, Betharam, and Bethnimrah, and Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, Jordan and his border, even unto the edge of the sea of Chinnereth on the other side Jordan eastward."

Num 32:34 — "And the children of Gad built Dibon, and Ataroth, and Aroer,"

Num 32:24 — "Build you cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep; and do that which hath proceeded out of your mouth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson joins care for the household to readiness for the battle.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the eastern tribes who built Beth-nimrah and its sister-cities. They housed their little ones and their flocks in fenced safety, and then crossed over armed to fight for their brethren. Provision for the family and readiness for the warfare of God’s people are not at odds; the godly man cares for his own household and yet does not excuse himself from the common battle.

Beth-nimrah, “house of sweet water,” also stands as a token of the LORD’s good provision. He gave His people a land of springs and pasture, fenced cities and folds, that they might dwell in safety. Every settled blessing of the believer’s life is from the same gracious hand; the sweet waters are His gift, and the house is built by His favour.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name joins beth, “house,” with a word for sweet water or for the leopard of the thickets.

expand to see more

Beth-nimrah — Hebrew Beth-Nimrah, “house of sweet water.”

By another sense the name means “house of the leopard.”

The prefix beth (“house”) opens many town-names.

It was built by the children of Gad in the valley.

The house of sweet water marks the LORD’s good provision for His people.

Usage

"Like Gad at Beth-nimrah, the godly join care for the household to readiness for the battle."

"Beth-nimrah teaches that the settled blessings of life are gifts of the LORD’s gracious hand."

"The house of sweet water marks the good provision God made for His people east of Jordan."
